The Carboniferous Period. Spanning from three hundred and fifty-nine to two hundred and ninety-nine million years ago, the Carboniferous was the age of vast swamp forests whose dead vegetation compacted into the coal deposits that gave the period its name. Giant insects, early reptiles, and early synapsids roamed the land. The atmosphere held nearly twice today's oxygen, enabling enormous arthropods to thrive. The supercontinent Pangaea was assembling during this time.

Enormous coal swamp forests dominated tropical continents, composed of giant club mosses, ferns, and conifers—the source of modern coal beds. Giant arthropods thrived in the oxygen-rich air, including dragonflies with wingspans of seventy centimetres and scorpions as large as dogs. Tetrapods diversified into early amphibians, still tied to water for breeding, and early reptiles with amniotic eggs, which enabled full land colonisation.

The first synapsids appeared during the Carboniferous—sail-backed creatures like Dimetrodon—representing the lineage leading to mammals. Oxygen levels reached roughly thirty-five percent of the atmosphere, compared to today's twenty-one percent, which enabled the size and activity of terrestrial life. The supercontinent Pangaea was forming as continents collided, creating equatorial rainforests that grew drier in the interior.

The Carboniferous follows the Devonian Period, when tetrapods first emerged, and precedes the Permian Period, when synapsids dominated and reptiles diversified further.
